Introduction

A plugin is a native dynamic library (.so on Linux, .dylib on macOS, .dll on Windows) that 3code loads at startup and calls at fixed points in its lifecycle: prompts, tool calls, turns, sessions. There is no manifest, no registration call, no RPC protocol. The library exports C functions; the host probes for them; whichever hooks exist get called. Each dynlib carries its own runtime, so a plugin can be written in anything that speaks the C ABI, and the reference SDK makes Nim one-file simple.

Reach for a plugin when you want machinery on the host side of the agent: policy (veto writes to frozen paths, redact secrets from tool output), instrumentation (usage counters, audit logs, custom notifications), or a model-facing tool backed by your own code. For teaching the model something, a skill file is still the right tool: it costs nothing until used, while every plugin-registered tool schema rides along on every model request. Most plugins want both halves: a host-side hook implementation plus a small skill that tells the model how to drive it.

Plugins are native code running in-process with your full user rights. Install only libraries you trust, from sources you trust. The default sandbox already fences the model out of the lib directories, so an agent cannot install one for you.

The model in one page

Discovery and load:

  1. $XDG_DATA_HOME/3code/lib (~/.local/share/3code/lib on Linux)
  2. /usr/local/lib/3code, /usr/lib/3code (Linux; %ProgramFiles%\3code\lib on Windows)

An optional [plugins] lib = path dir is scanned first. Files are sorted by name within each directory; on a stem collision the first match wins. A candidate that does not export tc_abi_version, or whose version differs from the host's, is skipped and noted in :plugins. Load order is the resulting sorted order, and load order is hook call order.

Everything else follows from one design decision: all plugin code runs on a single dedicated host thread, one call at a time, in load order. Never on the turn, net, or input threads; a plugin never needs locks of its own to be safe against the host. Sync hooks (prompt, system prompt, tool pre/result/exec, init/register/shutdown) round-trip with a deadline, so a slow plugin cannot stall a turn forever. Async hooks (turn, session, compact, file-write events) are fire-and-forget copies into a bounded queue.

Multiple plugins chain: mutations waterfall in load order (plugin two sees plugin one's edit), a veto or takeover short-circuits the chain and names the plugin in the tool result.

Writing a plugin: the short manual

The shape of a module

One Nim file. The ABI types first, your hook procs in the middle, the SDK include last. The SDK include is what turns your onPrompt into the exported tc_on_prompt the host probes for, and it registers the host's plugin thread with your library's garbage collector before your first allocation:

include threecode/pluginabi   # types + helpers (FIRST)
import std/[json, os]         # your imports

proc onPrompt*(ev: var TcPromptEvent) =
  if "deploy" in tcView(ev.prompt):
    tcAssignStr(ev.prompt, tcView(ev.prompt) & "\n[checked by myplugin]")

include threecode/plugin_sdk   # exports the tc_* hooks (LAST)

Define any subset of the optional procs; only defined ones are exported and thus subscribed by the host. Hook filtering (say, only some tools) is your job, not the host's: a cheap if tcView(ev.name) != "write": return guard at the top is the intended idiom.

Build and install (the ABI modules come from the 3code source tree; -p: it in, or use an installed package):

nim c --app:lib --mm:orc --threads:on -p:~/p/3code/src -o:myplugin.so myplugin.nim
cp myplugin.so ~/.local/share/3code/lib/

--threads:on is not optional: the host calls you from its own thread, and without the SDK's foreign-thread registration your first allocation there is undefined behavior. Run :plugins to confirm the load (it lists subscribed hooks and call counts), then :plugin debug on to watch it live.

Editing data in place

Read a field with tcView, replace it with tcAssignStr. The buffer you may grow is capped (see strings and buffers); an edit that does not fit is dropped and the host logs it. Do not write past len, do not free anything, do not retain a pointer after your proc returns: every pointer the host hands you is valid only for the duration of the call.

Steering tool calls

onToolPre sees every tool call before execution and returns a verdict:

proc onToolPre*(ev: var TcToolPreEvent): cint =
  if tcView(ev.name) == "write" and "migrations" in tcView(ev.args):
    tcAssignStr(ev.message, "myplugin: migrations are frozen today")
    return tcVeto
  tcAllow

  • tcAllow (0): proceed unchanged.
  • tcVeto (1): skip the call; message becomes the tool result the model sees.
  • tcRewrite (2): you edited args (JSON text); proceed with the new ones.
  • tcTakeover (3): skip execution; message and code are the whole result. You did the work yourself, which runs outside the sandbox, with your full rights. That is the point, and the risk.
  • tcWrap (4): run the original, sandboxed, with message prepended and post appended to its output. Multiple wraps compose in load order.

onToolResult fires after a call lands and can edit the output before the model reads it (redaction is the classic use) and even the exit code.

Registering a model-facing tool

Two procs cooperate: one registers, one executes.

proc registerTools*(s: ptr TcState) =
  discard s.registerTool("weather", "current conditions",
    """{"type":"function","function":{"name":"weather",
       "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{
         "city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}}}""")

proc onToolExec*(ev: var TcToolExecEvent): int32 =
  tcAssignStr(ev.output, "sunny")
  0

registerTool is legal only inside registerTools. The schema is an OpenAI function-tool definition; the name must not collide with a builtin tool (bash, read, write, ... check :plugins for rejections) or an already-registered one. The optional last argument is a per-call timeout in milliseconds; 0 means the host default (120 s).

Tools are advertised to the model only when [plugins] tools = "on", which is deliberately off by default: the tool array is stateless and rides every model request, so every registered schema is billed on every call whether used or not, roughly 300-900 tokens for a small curated one. The gate makes mounting a deliberate choice. Executions run unsandboxed in the plugin, like any plugin code. Drop a skill in ~/.config/3code/skills/myplugin.md teaching the model when and how to call the tool; that is the whole install convention.

Long work and interruption

A sync hook that runs long gets its default outcome applied without it (see failure handling). Poll tcCancelled(tcCurrentState) in any loop that might outlive its budget, including tool execs (Esc during a turn sets the flag):

while moreWork() and not tcCancelled(tcCurrentState):
  doChunk()

Beyond Nim

The ABI is plain C. A plugin in C, Rust (extern "C"), Zig, or anything else just exports the tc_* symbols itself, honors abi/structSize (treat a larger host struct as trailing unknown bytes; refuse nothing except a structSize smaller than yours), and keeps the memory rules above. The fixture in tests/testdata/plugin_fixture.nim in the 3code repo is the canonical worked example of every hook, heavily commented.

Async means fire-and-forget: the host copies a small POD event into a bounded queue (256 entries, oldest dropped under pressure) and moves on. Do not mutate async events as if the host were waiting; it is not.

Event structs. TcStr fields are read-only views; TcMutStr fields may be edited in place. Every struct also carries abi and structSize first.

TcPromptEvent: prompt (mut, 1 MiB), cwd, sessionPath, provider, model.

TcSysPromptEvent: prompt (mut, 512 KiB), provider, model, family. The result is cached per (provider, model, family) for the process lifetime.

TcToolPreEvent: name, callId, family; args (mut, 256 KiB, JSON text of the tool arguments); out fields verdict, message (4 KiB), post (4 KiB), code. Set the verdict by returning it.

TcToolResultEvent: name, args, elapsedMs, diff (the bash-style diff when a tool produced one); output (mut, 1 MiB) and code (pointer, editable) shape what the model sees.

TcToolExecEvent: name, args; out fields output (mut, 1 MiB) and code. Your whole job: fill output, return the exit code as ev.code (the proc's return value).

TcTurnEvent: turn, promptTokens, cwd.

TcTurnEndEvent: turn, promptTokens, completionTokens, reasoningTokens, elapsedMs, interrupted, sessionPath.

TcRetryEvent: provider, model, status (HTTP status or 0), category, backoffS, attempt.

TcSessionEvent: sessionPath, cwd, provider, model, resumed, messages.

TcCompactEvent: before, after (message counts), summary.

TcFileWriteEvent: path (project-relative when possible), bytes, kind (0 write, 1 patch, 2 apply_patch).

Strings and buffers

TcStr is a read-only data+len view into host memory, not NUL-terminated. TcMutStr is a host-allocated buffer with len <= cap at all times. tcView copies a view into a Nim string (the only allocating conversion; call it when you need the bytes), tcAssignStr copies your bytes back, silently doing nothing when they do not fit cap (the host logs the drop).

The host sizes each editable buffer at twice the payload, floored at 16 KiB, capped per field: prompt 1 MiB, system prompt 512 KiB, tool args 256 KiB, tool result and tool-exec output 1 MiB, tool-pre message/post 4 KiB. A payload already over its cap skips the hook entirely rather than truncating silently; the debug trace shows the skip. Ordinary edits always fit.

State, services, cancellation

TcState is the per-plugin context the host passes as the first argument everywhere. It is stable for the process lifetime, so a pointer stashed in userData survives between calls. Fields: abi, structSize, pluginName, userData, cancelled (set to 1 by the host when the user interrupts while your call is in flight), and services.

TcServices are host callables:

  • log(msg): append to the debug trace, tagged with your plugin name. Safe from any hook.
  • registerTool(name, description, schemaJson, timeoutMs): legal only inside registerTools. Returns 0 on success, 1 outside registration, 2 for an empty name, 3 for a builtin tool name, 4 for a duplicate. The Nim-side s.registerTool(...) wrapper returns a bool.

The SDK keeps the current call's state pointer in the threadvar tcCurrentState; tcCancelled(tcCurrentState) is the polite way to poll for interruption.

Failure handling

A sync hook has a deadline (2 s, or the tool-exec budget; the env vars THREECODE_PLUGIN_SYNC_MS and THREECODE_PLUGIN_TOOL_MS retune them). On timeout the default outcome applies without you: allow for verdicts, the original text for prompts and outputs, an error result for a plugin tool. The plugin takes a strike, the host flags cancelled so a well-behaved hook winds down, and three strikes demote the plugin: its sync hooks are skipped for the rest of the session (:plugins shows DEMOTED). A Nim exception in a hook is caught and traced; a segfault takes the process down. There is no process isolation in this tier, which is why the lib directories are yours, not the model's.

Config and debug

keyeffect
disable = "slow, other"skip plugins by lib file stem
tools = "on"advertise registered tools to the model (opt-in)
debug = "on"per-call trace with mutation diffs
lib = "/path"extra discovery dir, scanned first

:plugins (or :plugin list) reports loaded libraries, subscribed hooks, call counts, strikes, registered tools, and every load-time skip with its reason. :plugin debug on traces every call to THREECODE_DEBUG_LOG (or stderr): the hook, the plugin, elapsed milliseconds, verdicts, and a line diff of anything a plugin mutated, which is the fastest way to see your plugin actually doing something.

ABI stability

The ABI version is 1 and must match exactly; a mismatched library is skipped, never shimmed. Additive changes (trailing struct fields) bump nothing: structSize negotiation absorbs them, and both sides treat a larger counterpart struct as unknown trailing bytes. Any incompatible layout or signature change bumps TcAbiVersion, and old plugins are refused loudly at load rather than corrupting memory quietly.
